principles.name: Spaced Repetition
principles.description: Reviewing material at systematically increasing intervals so that each review occurs just as memory strength begins to decline.
principles.mechanism: The spacing effect shows that distributing practice over time produces stronger and more durable long-term memory traces than massed practice, because each retrieval attempt at the point of near-forgetting forces effortful reconstruction that deepens encoding.
principles.source: Cepeda, N. J., Pashler, H., Vul, E., Wixted, J. T., & Rohrer, D. (2006). Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks: A review and quantitative synthesis. Psychological Bulletin, 132(3), 354–380. (Original phenomenon: Ebbinghaus, H. (1913). Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology. Teachers College, Columbia University. Original work published 1885.)
principles.example: Use a flashcard app (e.g., Anki) that automatically schedules each vocabulary card for the optimal review day — new cards daily, older cards at expanding intervals.

principles.name: Interleaving
principles.description: Mixing different topics or problem types within a single study session rather than completing all problems of one type before moving to the next.
principles.mechanism: Switching between categories forces the learner to discriminate between problem types and retrieve the appropriate strategy each time, building flexible, transferable knowledge rather than surface pattern recognition.
principles.source: Kornell, N., & Bjork, R. A. (2008). Learning concepts and categories: Is spacing the 'enemy of induction'? Psychological Science, 19(6), 585–592.
principles.example: When practising mathematics, alternate between algebra, geometry, and statistics problems in one session rather than completing a full chapter of each subject separately.

principles.name: Retrieval Practice
principles.description: Actively recalling information from memory — through quizzes, free recall, or practice tests — rather than passively re-reading source material.
principles.mechanism: The act of retrieving a memory strengthens that memory more than restudying does (the testing effect), because effortful retrieval modifies the memory trace itself and improves future accessibility.
principles.source: Roediger, H. L., & Karpicke, J. D. (2006). Test-enhanced learning: Taking memory tests improves long-term retention. Psychological Science, 17(3), 249–255.
principles.example: After reading a textbook chapter, close the book and write down everything you can recall; then check your notes against the text to identify gaps.

principles.name: Elaborative Interrogation
principles.description: Generating explanations for facts by asking and answering 'why is this true?' and 'how does this connect to what I already know?'
principles.mechanism: Elaborative interrogation forces the learner to integrate new information with prior knowledge, creating a richer network of associations that provides multiple retrieval routes and deepens semantic understanding.
principles.source: Pressley, M., Symons, S., McDaniel, M. A., Snyder, B. L., & Turnure, J. E. (1988). Elaborative interrogation facilitates acquisition of confusing facts. Journal of Educational Psychology, 80(3), 268–278. (See also Pressley, M., et al. (1992). Encouraging mindful use of prior knowledge: Attempting to construct explanatory answers facilitates learning. Applied Cognitive Psychology, 6(1), 1–18.)
principles.example: While studying the circulatory system, pause at each fact and ask 'Why does blood need to be pumped under pressure?' and generate your own explanation before reading further.

principles.name: Implementation Intention
principles.description: Forming a specific when–where–how plan for a desired behaviour using the format 'When situation X occurs, I will perform response Y'.
principles.mechanism: Pre-deciding the exact context bridges the intention–action gap by creating a mental link between a situational cue and the intended response, reducing deliberation at the moment of action.
principles.source: Gollwitzer, P. M. (1999). Implementation intentions: Strong effects of simple plans. American Psychologist, 54(7), 493–503.
principles.example: When the train doors close on my morning commute, I will open my language-learning app and complete exactly one lesson before checking any messages.

principles.name: Deliberate Practice
principles.description: Engaging in highly structured, effortful practice that targets specific weaknesses just beyond current ability, with immediate feedback on errors.
principles.mechanism: Expert performance results from sustained, focused practice at the edge of competence — this challenge level maximises neural plasticity and skill encoding, which passive or comfortable practice does not produce.
principles.source: Ericsson, K. A., Krampe, R. T., & Tesch-Römer, C. (1993). The role of deliberate practice in the acquisition of expert performance. Psychological Review, 100(3), 363–406.
principles.example: A guitarist who consistently struggles with chord transitions practises only those transitions slowly with a metronome for 20 focused minutes, not by playing easy full songs.

principles.name: Chunking
principles.description: Grouping individual pieces of information into larger meaningful units so that each chunk can be processed as a single cognitive entity.
principles.mechanism: Because working memory can hold only a limited number of items simultaneously, organising information into familiar higher-order chunks compresses the effective load and frees capacity for higher-level reasoning and pattern recognition.
principles.source: Miller, G. A. (1956). The magical number seven, plus or minus two: Some limits on our capacity for processing information. Psychological Review, 63(2), 81–97. (Application: Oakley, B. (2014). A Mind for Numbers: How to Excel at Math and Science. TarcherPerigee.)
principles.example: When learning programming syntax, group related functions into conceptual clusters (e.g., 'string manipulation methods') and learn the cluster as a unit rather than individual commands in isolation.
